title: A NHANES Survey-Based Homebound Proxy and Mortality Among Older Adults in the United States: Up to 20 Years of Follow-Up in NHANES 1999–2004
content: Homebound status is a requirement for Medicare home health eligibility, and home healthcare clinicians assess it at the start of every episode of care. Older adults who are homebound have higher mortality than those who are not, but less is known about whether this association changes over time or persists after accounting for functional limitation and underlying disease. This study followed 4,262 adults aged 60 years and older from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999–2004 for up to 20 years through linked death records. A NHANES survey-based homebound proxy was defined from two items: use of special equipment because of a health problem, and much difficulty or inability to go out for activities such as shopping, movies, or sporting events. Overall, 259 participants (6.1%) met both criteria. In unweighted estimates for the analytic sample, 13.5% of these participants died within 1 year, compared with 1.4% of those meeting neither criterion. After adjustment for demographics, chronic conditions, laboratory values, and cardiac biomarkers, meeting both criteria was associated with a higher hazard of death in the first 5 years (hazard ratio [HR] 2.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.97–3.02). The association attenuated but remained after further adjustment for a count of other functional limitations (HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.20–2.10). After deaths before 24 months were excluded, the HR from 2 to 5 years was 1.98 (95% CI 1.50–2.61), and the estimate adjusted for other limitations was smaller and less precise (HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.88–1.78). Associations after 5 years were weaker and less certain. Older adults who met both criteria had high mortality during the first 5 years of follow-up. For home healthcare clinicians, these findings support early care coordination, rehabilitation, and goals-of-care conversations for patients who have substantial difficulty leaving home, with decisions guided by individual assessment.
